newsitem.title: USA: Rockwell says on target for 15 pct EPS.
newsitem.headline: Rockwell says on target for 15 pct EPS.

text.p: Rockwell International Corp chairman Don Beall said Monday his company is on target to meet its goal of 15 percent annual earnings per share growth for the next five years with automation and avionics and communications driving 1997 profits.

Commenting on the company's first quarter earnings, Beall told reporters, "Our goals for the average year are growing revenues in the eight percent range and earnings per share in the 15 percent range, this has got us off to a good start to meet those goals."
Seal Beach, Calif.-based Rockwell reported an 18 percent jump in operating profits Monday.
"We're looking for automation to have a good year and to be a major factor in the year-to-year improvement in the company," Beall said.

"Avionics is having ... an even better year. It's market improvement is driven largely by the commercial air transport market ... (which) is clearly on a long-term cyclical uptrend and we will see continued improvement from that part of our business this year," he said.

The Seal Beach, Calif.-based company, reported a profit of $179 million, or $0.82 a share, in the first quarter ended in December, up from operating profits of $152 million, or $0.70 a share in the year-ago period. Sales rose nine percent to $2.6 billion from $2.4 billion. Discontinued operations provided $40 million in income in the year ago first quarter.

This quarter is the first since Rockwell sold its aerospace and defense businesses to Boeing Co for $3.2 billion in December to focus on higher growth sectors. The company is now mainly a commercial electronics firm.

Beall told reporters that after the sale to Boeing only five percent of its revenues comes from the U.S. government. Just one year ago one quarter of Rockwell's revenues came from the U.S. government, a decade ago two out of every three of its revenue dollars came from the U.S. government.
Beall said that the company's three electronics businesses, automation, avionics and communications and semiconductor systems will continue to drive growth.

"The greatest growth will come from the electronics businesses," Beall said noting that the industries those businesses sell their products to are growing faster than the more mature automotive industry.

Profits in the company's semiconductor business were $81 million in the first quarter, up from $80 million in the year-ago period due to lower modem prices and higher expenses as the company moves to its new 56 kilobit per second modems which it is hoping to establish as the new industry standard.
Rockwell is launching a 56 kilobit per second modem in direct competition to the "x2" technology being sold by U.S. Robotics Corp.
"We've got a real horse race here in the 56 kilobit world," Beall said.

The two firms have yet to agree on a set of standards that would allow the two modem technologies to communicate with one another. That could mean potential problems for consumers when they upgrade to the faster modems.

"We're very focused on accelerating the (development) of a standard ... we're going to have a period of some uncertaintly as these new products roll out, but this is an important business to us and we intend to play a leadership role in it," he said.
Beall said Rockwell will continue to consider making acquisitions to grow its business.

"We're looking at many possibilities all the time but the most likely scenario is for us to do small to medium size product line ... acquisitions to support these terrific franchises that represent Rockwell's business today," he said.
